title: Stress, Strain, Elasticity and Plasticity
notes: **Stress (σ):** the internal resisting force per unit area set up in a body when external forces are applied: σ = F/A. Empirical units are N/m² or Pa (pascal). Normal stress = force perpendicular to the area (tension/compression); shear stress = force parallel to the area.

**Strain (ε):** the fractional deformation produced: strain = change in dimension / original dimension. It is dimensionless. Linear strain = Δl/l, shear strain = θ (angle of shear), volumetric strain = ΔV/V.

**Elasticity and plasticity:** elasticity is the property of a body to regain its original shape and size when the deforming force is removed. Plasticity is the property of remaining permanently deformed after the deforming force is removed. Bodies are elastic below the elastic limit and plastic beyond it.

**Hooke's law in stress-strain form:** within the elastic limit, stress ∝ strain: σ = Eε, where E is Young's modulus (N/m²). This is the generalised Hooke's law — stress and strain are proportional until the elastic limit.

**Stress-strain curve regions:** (1) linear (proportional) region up to the proportional limit; (2) elastic region up to the elastic limit (still recovers fully); (3) yielding at the yield point (permanent deformation begins); (4) plastic deformation region where the material flows; (5) ultimate tensile strength (maximum stress), then (6) fracture/breaking point.

**Worked example — a wire under tension:** a steel wire of length 2 m and cross-section 1 mm² (10⁻⁶ m²) carries a 20 kg load. F = 196 N, σ = 196/10⁻⁶ = 1.96 × 10⁸ Pa. If E_steel = 2 × 10¹¹ Pa, strain ε = σ/E = 9.8 × 10⁻⁴, so extension Δl = 9.8 × 10⁻⁴ × 2 = 1.96 mm.

**Types of stress & strain (NEB focus):** tensile/compressive (longitudinal), shear (tangential), and volume (hydrostatic). Each has its own modulus: Young's modulus E = σ_t/ε_l, shear modulus G = τ/θ, bulk modulus B = −P/(ΔV/V).

**Ductile vs brittle materials:** ductile (copper, mild steel) show a long plastic region — they deform before breaking and are used for wires. Brittle (glass, cast iron) show little or no plastic region — they break suddenly near the elastic limit, which is why glass shatters.
confusion: ❌ 'Stress and pressure are the same.' ✅ Both have units N/m², but stress is the INTERNAL resisting force per unit area produced in a body, while pressure is an EXTERNAL force per unit area applied by a fluid.
❌ 'Strain has units.' ✅ Strain is dimensionless — it is a ratio of lengths (or volumes/angles). This is essential for dimensional analysis.
❌ 'Elasticity means materials are always elastic.' ✅ Every material is elastic only up to its elastic limit; beyond it, plastic deformation occurs.
❌ 'Stress equals force.' ✅ Stress is force PER unit area (σ = F/A). Doubling the area halves the stress for the same force.
❌ 'The stress–strain graph is a straight line everywhere.' ✅ Only up to the proportional limit. After that it curves at the yield point and beyond.
❌ 'A ductile material breaks near the elastic limit.' ✅ DUCTILE materials deform plastically and stretch before fracturing; brittle materials break with little warning near the elastic limit.

universalFacts: Stress and strain were first quantified by Robert Hooke and later generalised by Thomas Young, after whom Young's modulus is named.
The area under the stress–strain curve equals the energy absorbed per unit volume (toughness) — important for crash safety design.
Stress is a tensor, not a scalar — it has components for tension, compression and shear in every direction.
Bone is an adaptation of stress engineering: it is strongest in compression and weakest in shear, matching the stresses the body faces.
The elastic limit and yield point coincide for many materials; for mild steel there is a distinct upper and lower yield point.
examples: Stress: A 1000 N force on a 5 cm² bar gives σ = 1000/(5×10⁻⁴) = 2×10⁶ Pa.
Strain: A wire stretched from 2.00 m to 2.01 m has ε = 0.01/2 = 5×10⁻³.
Young's modulus: σ = 1.96×10⁸ Pa, ε = 9.8×10⁻⁴ → E = 2×10¹¹ N/m² (steel).
Shear: A force parallel to the top face of a cube displaces it — shear stress τ = F/A, shear strain θ.
Volume: Pressure P on a sphere → B = −P/(ΔV/V). For water, B ≈ 2.2×10⁹ Pa.

formulas: Strain: ε = Δl/l (dimensionless; ε_V = ΔV/V, shear ε = θ)
Hooke's law in stress–strain form: σ = Eε
Bulk modulus: B = −P/(ΔV/V); Shear modulus: G = τ/θ
keyPoints: Stress is force per unit area; strain is fractional deformation (dimensionless).
Elasticity = recovery of shape when the force is removed; plasticity = permanent deformation.
Stress is proportional to strain only within the elastic limit (Hooke's law, σ = Eε).
The stress–strain curve has six regions: proportional, elastic, yield, plastic, ultimate, fracture.
Ductile materials deform plastically before breaking; brittle ones break suddenly near the elastic limit.
summary: Stress (σ = F/A) and strain (ε = Δl/l) describe how solids respond to deforming forces. Within the elastic limit, σ = Eε (Hooke's law). Elastic bodies recover their shape; plastic bodies deform permanently. The stress–strain curve shows the proportional limit, elastic limit, yield point, ultimate strength and fracture — ductile materials deform plastically first, brittle materials shatter suddenly.
specialNotes: Strain is dimensionless — never attach units.
Stress and pressure share the N/m² unit but are different concepts (internal vs external).
The elastic limit is the maximum stress from which the body still recovers fully.
For safety design, working stress is kept well below the yield/ultimate stress (safety factor).
NEB frequently asks to label the stress–strain curve and to calculate E from a numerical.
importantStatements: Stress is the internal force per unit area resisting deformation: σ = F/A.
Strain is the fractional change in dimension and is dimensionless: ε = Δl/l.
Within the elastic limit stress is proportional to strain (Hooke's law): σ = Eε.
Elasticity is the property of recovering original shape; plasticity is permanent deformation.
Young's modulus E = Fl/(AΔl) quantifies the stiffness of a material in tension.
importantNotes: Always distinguish stress (F/A) from strain (Δl/l) — one has units, one is dimensionless.
The elastic limit is the boundary between recoverable (elastic) and permanent (plastic) deformation.
σ = Eε is the stress–strain form of Hooke's law and holds only within the elastic limit.
The area under the stress–strain curve is the toughness — the energy absorbed per unit volume.
Ductility and brittleness are read directly from the length of the plastic region of the curve.
examShortTricks: Remember: strain has NO units — a quick sanity check for MCQs.
To find E: rearrange to E = Fl/(AΔl) — compute σ then divide by ε.
Stress–strain curve order: proportional → elastic → yield → plastic → ultimate → fracture.
Compression increases density; bulk modulus B = −P/(ΔV/V) is positive because ΔV is negative.
For breaking load: F_max = σ_break × A — stress times the area.
examNotes: Stress and strain numericals are a guaranteed exam topic — practice unit conversions (mm² → m²).
Labeling the stress–strain curve and identifying regions carries direct marks.
Young's modulus problems (extension of a wire) appear almost every year.
Bulk modulus and shear modulus are often asked as short-answer comparisons.
Safety factor = ultimate stress / working stress — a common applied question.
